title: An orderly account (Luke 1:1–4)
hookLine: Luke, a careful researcher, writes to Theophilus, friend of God

lines: NINETY DAYS, ONE GOSPEL, IN ORDER.
MARK SHOUTS, JOHN SOARS, MATTHEW LISTS.
cards: For the next ninety days, this path does something simple and rare: it reads one Gospel, Luke, from beginning to end, in order. Not just the well-known bits. The whole thing.
And Luke starts like no other Gospel. Mark begins with a shout in the wilderness. John begins in eternity: in the beginning was the Word.
Matthew begins with a family tree. Luke begins like a careful researcher writing a cover letter: how he worked, where his material came from, and why he's writing.
Four verses, and you can almost hear him tapping his notes into a neat pile.

teach.b: Here's how it opens, in the King James Bible: "Forasmuch as many have taken in hand to set forth in order a declaration of those things which are most surely believed among us."
Luke admits others have written about Jesus already.
Then his sources: those "which from the beginning were eyewitnesses, and ministers of the word."
Then his method: he writes as one "having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first," setting it down in order.
And his purpose: "That thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed."

Notice who he's writing to: most excellent Theophilus. Nobody knows for sure who he was. Most excellent is the title the book of Acts gives a Roman governor, Felix, so Theophilus may have been a person of rank.
But his name means friend of God, or loved by God, and some readers wonder whether Luke means every reader who loves God. Either way, Luke wrote him a second volume: Acts opens with his name again.
And who was Luke? The Gospel never names its author.
Early Christian tradition says it was Luke, a physician and traveling companion of Paul, and the letter to the Colossians, under Paul's name, mentions Luke, the beloved physician.

teach.h: THAT THOU MIGHTEST KNOW THE CERTAINTY.
teach.b: Some hold that tradition firmly; others weigh it differently. What the text itself shows is the method. Luke wants Theophilus to know this isn't rumor: he followed it all from the start.

how: Some Christians read a Gospel straight through, a chapter a day, and churches following the common lectionary read mainly from Luke in one year of their three-year cycle.

games.q: you're Luke. others have already written about Jesus. you want Theophilus to be sure of what he's been taught. what do you do?
o: follow everything closely from the start and write it in order.
copy the longest account you can find.
games.why: he gathers what the eyewitnesses passed on, follows it from the very first, and writes it in order, "that thou mightest know the certainty."

practice: Bring to mind one thing that happened to you that you don't want to lose: a conversation, a kindness, a turning point, something a grandparent told you.

Walk through it from the beginning, in order, the way Luke gathered what the eyewitnesses said: who was there, what was said, what it changed. If you pray, give thanks for that moment; if not, simply hold it with care.

wordCard.voice: Theophilus, meaning friend of God: the man Luke writes to, with a careful, researched telling of Jesus, set down in order from the eyewitnesses.

orig.note: Greek: friend of God, or loved by God. the man Luke writes to, and perhaps every reader.
